html:
From 1864 to 1904 the Russian Empire banned books and newspapers in Lithuanian printed in the Latin alphabet, allowing only Cyrillic. Lithuanians resisted by smuggling books.

The ban followed the uprising of 1863 against Russian rule and aimed to pull Lithuanians away from Poland and Catholicism. Instead, presses in East Prussia printed Lithuanian books, and book smugglers, the knygnešiai, carried them across the border at great risk. Catholic priests and secret home schools taught children to read.

The ban failed and was lifted in 1904. It made literacy and the Lithuanian language a cause, and the smugglers became national heroes. The movement it fed led to the declaration of independence in 1918. It was part of the Russification of the empire's western lands. See Lithuania.
sum: From 1864 to 1904 the Russian Empire banned books and newspapers in Lithuanian printed in the Latin alphabet, allowing only Cyrillic. Lithuanians resisted by smuggling books.
